https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-a.text: BRUSSELS — Russian drones attacked a crossing point on the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday morning, hitting a passenger train two kilometers from the frontier in Volyn Oblast. Ukraine’s state rail operator confirmed that a strike hit the locomotive of a passenger train bound for Warsaw. The train crew were warned of the threat in advance by Ukrainian authorities and no one was injured, the operator added. Separately, social media videos showed a large fire at a gas station near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing point between Ukraine and Poland. According to local media, there are no reports yet of casualties from the gas station fire. Advertisement Advertisement Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to the border strikes with a post on X stating that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.” “Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Sybiha added, urging Ukraine’s allies to “throw the full weight of your sanctions at Putin’s aggressive regime.” Attacks on the EU’s borders have intensified as some intelligence agencies warn of a buildup towards a direct attack by Russia on a NATO member country. Europe faces “an escalating campaign of threats” and “hybrid warfare,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month. Russia’s “hybrid war” campaign has also been linked to an explosive-laden drone found near Leipzig airport in Germany, a sea drone later blown up by Romania in the Black Sea, and reports of a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of German arms producer Rheinmetall.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The San Bernardino county sheriff’s department cold homicide case submitted the remains for DNA identification in 2023. Photograph: Felipe Sanchez/Alamy View image in fullscreen The San Bernardino county sheriff’s department cold homicide case submitted the remains for DNA identification in 2023. Photograph: Felipe Sanchez/Alamy California California man charged in the killing of his ex-wife – two decades after she vanished Authorities discovered a body hidden in a home’s crawlspace in 2020, 13 years after Jill Maiorca disappeared Ramon Antonio Vargas Sat 26 Sep 2026 11.28 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 11.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man was recently charged in California with the killing of his ex-wife six years after her remains were discovered in a crawlspace beneath a home – and about two decades after when she went missing, according to investigators. Jeff Maiorca, 53, faces a charge of murder in the death of Jill Maiorca, who was 29 when she was killed, authorities said in discussing what could be one of the latest cases in the US to be solved with modern DNA techniques. Jill Maiorca’s disappearance was reported in the southern California city of Big Bear Lake in 2007, a statement from the local San Bernardino county sheriff’s department said. Jill Maiorca in an undated photo. Photograph: Courtesy of the San Bernardino county sheriff's department The path to finding Jill Maiorca then began in late October 2020, when San Bernardino sheriff’s deputies received a call to investigate “a suspicious discovery in the crawlspace under [a] residence” in Big Bear Lake. The deputies and members of the Big Bear fire department ultimately located human remains in that crawlspace. Although the remains couldn’t immediately be identified, an autopsy determined the manner of death in the case was homicide, the San Bernardino sheriff’s office statement said. The agency said its cold homicide case team in 2023 then submitted the unidentified remains for additional investigative DNA analysis. Such analysis determined the remains were those of Jill Maiorca, according to the sheriff’s office. The sheriff’s office also said that its investigators had come to consider Jeff Maiorca – who had been Jill’s husband and had filed to divorce her in 2004, court records showed – as a suspect. Citing unspecified evidence, the sheriff’s office’s statement asserted that Jill Maiorca had been murdered in November 2006. Her remains were then concealed – “without the homeowner’s knowledge” – beneath the residence where they were later discovered, the sheriff’s office said. The agency did not elaborate on the hiding of Jill Maiorca’s body. Business records reviewed by the Guardian link Jeff Maiorca to a heating, ventilation and air conditioning company. Other records showed his divorce from Jill Maiorca was classified as one involving children. The San Bernardino sheriff’s office said it arrested Maiorca on Monday. He was formally charged with murder as well as with the use of a deadly weapon, and he had an initial hearing on Wednesday in San Bernardino county superior court, as NBC News first reported. Jeff Maiorca remained in custody on Saturday at the High Desert jail in Adelanto, California , records indicated. Multiple media outlets reported that he was being held there without bail, and he was tentatively scheduled to appear in court again on 12 October. https://www.governmentnews.com.au/the-di.text: Technology 0 by Christopher Kelly September 17, 2026 September 18, 2026 (iStock.com/StockImages_AT) With 100 percent of public services online, Estonia is considered to have the world’s most digitised government. The transition was made early – the state introduced electronic cabinet meetings in 2000. The government also established an online tax filing system – the e-Tax Board. The system enables Estonians to file their income tax returns in just a few minutes. A year later Estonia introduced X-Road – open-source software that creates a secure data exchange between different departments. When one agency requires a piece of information held by another, X-Road handles the exchange through an encrypted pathway. Every access is recorded, and citizens can log in and see which government body looked at their data and when. Then came the mandatory digital ID. Since 2002, every Estonian resident over the age of 15 has been required to hold a digital identity card. Held by around 98 per cent of eligible citizens, the digital ID is a legal proof of identity and a one-stop login for online government services. Estonians use the ID to file taxes, access their medical records, sign official documents, and vote in elections. More recently, Estonia established a Digital Society Development Plan. Approved in May, the document provides an updated strategic framework for digital governance. Additionally, there is an AI Ethics Advisory Council which guides the ethical use of artificial intelligence across the public sector and evaluates societal and rights-based implications. To protect the government from cyberattacks, a “data embassy” has been created – a secure physical server located in Luxembourg that operates under Estonian legal jurisdiction. The embassy has been designed not just to passively store data, but to run critical government services from abroad during a national crisis. The government claims the country’s digital infrastructure – which costs the state around 60 million euros a year to operate ($100m) – produces annual savings of about 2 per cent of GDP and saves 800 years of collective working time that would otherwise be spent processing paperwork, entering data, and on in-person bureaucracy across public sectors.
